nodes.title:
COUNTING 2 BILLION VIEWS
map:     each worker counts its chunk
shuffle: same video → same worker
reduce:  sum the counts per video
→ 100 workers: ~20 minutes

TAMING A HOT KEY
⚠ viral video: 800M rows → one reducer
→ combiner: each mapper sends 1 count
→ salting: 4f2#0 … 4f2#9 → 10 reducers
# job: 3 h → 20 min

EVENT TIME VS ARRIVAL TIME
view at 12:04, arrives 14:10
watermark: “events ≤ 5 min late”
⚠ 2 h late → correct window later
→ duplicate id → dropped

UNIQUE VIEWERS OF 4F2
exact: remember every viewer id
⚠ 50M ids × 16 bytes ≈ 800 MB
→ HyperLogLog: 12 KB, ~1% error
# sketches merge across machines

meta.title: Batch & Stream Processing
meta.summary: Crunching billions of events: overnight in big batches, or continuously as they arrive.

goals.text: Keep analytics off the production database

steps.title: Analytics on the production database
steps.body:
Every view of every video is a row in the production database — about 2 billion a day. A dashboard shows views per video, recomputed every minute with a big `GROUP BY`.

Each run scans the whole day so far — hundreds of millions of rows by mid-morning — and the database that serves the app grinds: viewers wait while it counts.

callout.text: Production databases are tuned for many small, fast queries. Huge scans steal their memory, CPU and disk.

steps.title: Batch: collect now, compute later
steps.body:
Instead, the app appends every view as an event to cheap **object storage** — files, not database rows. Once a night a [[batch job]] reads the whole day, computes the counts on a cluster of workers, and writes the results to an analytics **warehouse**.

The dashboard reads the warehouse. The production database only serves the app again.

callout.text: Batch is simple, cheap and easy to rerun: if the job had a bug, fix it and run it again over the same files.

steps.title: Split the work: map, shuffle, reduce
steps.body:
2 billion events won’t fit through one machine quickly, so the job is split. **Map**: each worker reads its own chunk of the files and counts views per video. **Shuffle**: counts for the same video are sent to the same worker. **Reduce**: that worker adds them up.

Add more workers and the job finishes proportionally faster.

callout.text: This is MapReduce. Today Spark, BigQuery, Snowflake and friends do the same thing behind a SQL interface.

steps.title: Case: one video, one exhausted reducer
steps.body:
One video went viral: 40% of all views yesterday. In the shuffle, every view of it goes to the *same* reducer. That worker grinds for 3 hours while the other 99 finished in 5 minutes — and the job waits for the slowest.

Splitting work by key only balances it if the keys are balanced. Real data rarely is.

callout.text: Skew is the most common reason a big batch job is mysteriously slow. Look for one task taking far longer than the rest.

steps.title: Combine early, split hot keys
steps.body:
Two standard fixes. A [[combiner]] pre-aggregates on each mapper: instead of shipping 800 million “view of 4f2” rows, every mapper sends one partial count. For keys that are still too hot, [[salting]] splits them — `4f2#0` … `4f2#9` go to ten reducers, and a final step adds the ten totals.

The job drops from 3 hours back to about 20 minutes.

callout.text: Spark and most SQL engines combine automatically for sums and counts, and can detect and split skewed keys for joins.

steps.title: A day late is too late
steps.body:
Some questions can’t wait for tonight. A video going viral should show up in “Trending” *now*. A bot farm faking millions of views should be caught in minutes, before it earns any money.

Running the batch job every hour helps a little, but each run still re-reads a huge pile of data.

callout.text: Batch answers “what happened?”. Some products need “what is happening?”.

changes: - Trending list is a day old

steps.title: Stream processing: compute as events arrive
steps.body:
Now the app publishes each view to an **event stream** (Kafka). A [[stream processor]] (Flink, Kafka Streams, Spark Streaming) reads events as they arrive and keeps running counts, writing results to a fast store.

The dashboard is seconds behind reality instead of a day.

callout.text: The processor keeps its counts in local state and checkpoints it regularly, so a crash resumes from the last checkpoint instead of from scratch.

steps.title: Counting in windows
steps.body:
A stream never ends, so “count views” needs a time frame: a [[window]]. **Tumbling** windows cut time into fixed slices (views per minute). **Sliding** windows overlap (views in the last 10 minutes, updated every minute).

A sudden jump between windows is exactly what “trending” — or fraud — looks like.

callout.text: Session windows group events by bursts of activity — useful for “how long did people watch?”.

steps.title: Case: late and duplicate events
steps.body:
A phone watches videos in the subway with no signal and uploads its views two hours later. Should they count for 12:04, when they happened, or now, when they arrived? And a flaky network makes some phones send the same event twice.

Stream processors use **event time** (when it happened), a [[watermark]] to decide when a window is complete enough to publish, a policy for stragglers, and an event id to drop duplicates.

callout.text: “Exactly-once” in streaming means checkpoints plus idempotent writes — the same lesson as queues, at billions of events a day.

steps.title: Case: the processor falls behind
steps.body:
A celebrity live stream triples traffic for an hour. The stream processor can’t keep up, and unprocessed events pile up in the stream: [[consumer lag]] reaches 4 minutes and 18 million events.

Nothing is lost — the stream keeps everything — but the “live” dashboard is now 4 minutes old, and the fraud check runs 4 minutes late.

callout.text: Consumer lag is the key health metric of any streaming system. Alert on it, in seconds or events.

steps.title: Scale out across partitions
steps.body:
The stream is split into **partitions** (by video id, so each video’s events stay in order). Each processor instance owns some partitions, so adding instances adds throughput: two processors, two partitions each.

The backlog drains, lag drops back to seconds, and an autoscaler can add processors whenever lag grows.

callout.text: The number of partitions caps the parallelism. Create more partitions than you need today — adding them later reshuffles keys.

steps.title: Case: counting unique viewers
steps.body:
Views are easy to count. **Unique** viewers are not: to count exactly you must remember every viewer id you’ve seen — 50 million ids for a popular video, about 800 MB of state, per video, per window.

A [[HyperLogLog]] sketch estimates the number of distinct ids in 12 KB with about 1% error, and sketches from different machines and windows simply merge.

callout.text: Approximate algorithms (HyperLogLog, count-min sketch, t-digest for percentiles) trade a tiny error for enormous savings. Dashboards rarely need the last 1%.

steps.title: Batch and stream, together
steps.body:
Many systems run both: a stream for fast, approximate answers and a nightly batch that recomputes the exact numbers from the full log (the **lambda architecture**).

Others keep only the stream and, to fix a bug or rebuild results, **replay** the retained event log through a new version of the processor (the **kappa architecture**).

• Freshness — Batch: Hours; Stream: Seconds
• Complexity — Batch: Low; Stream: Higher
• Rerun — Batch: Easy; Stream: Replay the log

callout.text: Start with batch unless you clearly need seconds. Add streaming for the few results that do.

changes: + Nightly batch back alongside the stream

steps.title: Recap
steps.body:
• Keep heavy analytics **off the production database**.
• **Batch**: process large, finished datasets cheaply — results are hours old.
• **Stream**: process events as they arrive — seconds old, more moving parts.
• Watch for **skewed keys** (combine, salt) and **consumer lag** (add partitions and processors).
• Handle **late** and **duplicate** events; many systems run **both**.

callout.text: That completes Architecture. Next module: **Security** — starting with authentication.
